1. Projecting amino acid changes onto transcript models

Source: vignettes/hla-a-lollipop-demo.Rmd
hla-a-lollipop-demo.Rmd

A dense landscape of HLA-A variation

This example summarizes 5,998 named HLA-A alleles, an MHC class I heavy chain, from IPD-IMGT/HLA release 3.66.0. Comparison with A*02:01:01:01 produces 1,212 amino-acid substitutions at 334 mature-protein residues. Each substitution has its own head, coloured by the alternative amino acid’s chemical group. Counts span 1–4,667, so logarithmic heights keep both rare and common alternatives visible.

The analysis includes every sequence in the pinned release that meets these explicit criteria:

  • A complete 365-residue precursor using only the twenty standard amino acids.
  • An allele name ending in a numeric field, excluding names with letter suffixes.
  • The same gap pattern as the reference in the official protein alignment.

All 5,998 sequences passing the first two criteria also pass the alignment check. Thus, equal length is verified against aligned residue coordinates, rather than assumed to imply positional correspondence. Partial sequences, other protein lengths, and ambiguous residues are outside this example’s scope.

Each named allele counts once, including named alleles encoding identical proteins. The panel contains 3,188 distinct mature protein sequences, but is not deduplicated to those proteins. Counts reflect database representation, not individuals, independent observations, or population frequencies.

Prepare one Syn object

Use one SynIndividual for the reference allele throughout this tutorial. It holds the reference FASTA and exon annotation, the reference protein, and two attached protein annotations:

  • hla_substitutions: counts of amino-acid alternatives, keyed to the reference transcript.
  • hla_regions: the six structural regions, using the same transcript key.

The example loader reads the bundled offline files, summarizes the alleles, and attaches these annotations. No separate mutation, domain, or exon tables need to be prepared before plotting.

library(ggexon)
library(ggplot2)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3

demo_dir <- system.file("extdata", "hla_a_lollipop", package = "ggexon")
source(file.path(demo_dir, "load-hla-a-example.R"), local = TRUE)
source(file.path(demo_dir, "plot-hla-a-example.R"), local = TRUE)
source(file.path(demo_dir, "project-hla-a-example.R"), local = TRUE)
hla <- load_hla_a_example(demo_dir)

class(hla)
#> [1] "SynIndividual"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ggexon"
class(get_annotation(hla, "hla_substitutions"))
#> [1] "SynProteinMutationAnnotation"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ggexon"
class(get_annotation(hla, "hla_regions"))
#> [1] "SynProteinDomainAnnotation"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ggexon"

hla is the object passed to every plot. The allele manifest, original protein sequences, residue-state counts, and source checksums are retained in the object’s metadata. hla_a_evidence(hla) retrieves them for inspection. They are supporting evidence, not separate plotting inputs. The helpers are example functions, rather than exported package functions.

data.frame(
  named_alleles = nrow(hla_a_evidence(hla)$alleles),
  distinct_mature_proteins = hla_a_evidence(hla)$distinct_mature_proteins,
  substitutions = nrow(query_protein_mutations(hla, annotation = "hla_substitutions")),
  variable_residues = length(unique(query_protein_mutations(
    hla, annotation = "hla_substitutions"
  )$mature_position))
)
#>   named_alleles distinct_mature_proteins substitutions variable_residues
#> 1          5998                     3188          1212               334

The allele manifest retains every exact name and sequence checksum. The original FASTA records are unchanged and bundled with gzip compression.

Protein coordinates and structural regions

The original precursor sequences include a 24-residue signal peptide. The plot uses mature-protein positions 1–341, so mature residue 156 is precursor residue 180. The signal peptide is excluded from comparison, while the original bundled sequences retain it.

The stored mutation position and structural start/end columns use precursor coordinates so they can be projected through the reference CDS. The same annotations also retain mature_position, mature_start, and mature_end columns. Selecting these columns gives the mature-protein view without creating a second set of annotations or changing the stored coordinates.

Structural boundaries come from the bundled UniProt P04439 snapshot, shifted by 24 residues. Its displayed sequence is A*03:01; only the shared structural boundaries annotate this equal-length HLA-A track. All substitutions are computed against the selected A*02:01 reference.

knitr::kable(as.data.frame(query_domains(get_annotation(hla, "hla_regions")))[,
  c("domain", "mature_start", "mature_end")],
  col.names = c("Protein region", "Mature start", "Mature end"))
Protein region Mature start Mature end
Alpha-1 1 90
Alpha-2 91 182
Alpha-3 183 274
Connecting peptide 275 284
Transmembrane 285 308
Cytoplasmic 309 341

CP denotes the connecting peptide, TM the transmembrane segment, and TAIL the cytoplasmic region. These are structural regions rather than all globular domains. Different DNA variants producing the same amino-acid change are grouped into one substitution. The protein view uses amino-acid coordinates; the gene-model section below projects them to the exact reference allele’s coding structure.

Dense lollipop summary 

plots <- plot_hla_a_example(hla)
#> Scale for y is already present.
#> Adding another scale for y, which will replace the existing scale.
#> Scale for y is already present.
#> Adding another scale for y, which will replace the existing scale.
plots$overview

All eligible named HLA-A alleles from the pinned release. Every substitution remains a separate head; colours describe the alternative amino acid, not its prevalence.

The plot has three deliberate layout choices:

  • Logarithmic counts. Head height is log10(allele_count + 1), matching ggexon’s mutation_y_trans = "log10" convention. Axis ticks show the original counts. This prevents thousands of common-allele counts from flattening singleton and low-count substitutions into the backbone.
  • Bounded local fanning. Heads at the same residue spread symmetrically within at most 1.6 residue units of that position. Fanning restarts at each residue, so dense early sites cannot push later heads beyond the protein. Every stem remains anchored to the actual residue.
  • Chemical-group colour. The alternative residues are grouped as aliphatic (A/V/I/L/M), aromatic (F/W/Y), polar (S/T/N/Q/C), basic (K/R/H), acidic (D/E), and glycine/proline (G/P). Exact alternative identities remain in the table.

At this density, some nearby heads can visually overlap, especially at equal counts. No substitutions are filtered or sampled out of the plot. The close-up and exported table provide exact values when the overview is too crowded.

The plot starts with ggexon(hla). geom_protein_lollipop() resolves the mutation and region annotations from that object during plot build. The core protein-coordinate recipe is:

ggexon(hla) +
  geom_protein_lollipop(
    annotation = "hla_substitutions", domain_annotation = "hla_regions",
    position = "mature_position", domain_start = "mature_start", domain_end = "mature_end",
    domain = "domain", protein_length = 341, protein_start = 1,
    mutation_y_by = "allele_count", mutation_y_trans = "log10",
    mutation_y_range = log10(c(1, 4667) + 1), spread_threshold = 0
  )

The dense example adds bounded fanning through ggplot2 layer data functions. Each function receives the plot’s hla object, queries its attached annotation, and computes stems or heads at build time. hla_a_lollipop_layout() applies symmetric offsets and retains every true residue anchor. This keeps the existing colour and transparency controls without passing precomputed plotting tables to ggexon(). Bounded fanning is specific to this example; the package’s default spreading API is unchanged.

head(query_protein_mutations(hla, annotation = "hla_substitutions")[,
  c("mutation", "allele_count", "n_alternatives", "amino_acid_group")])
#>   mutation allele_count n_alternatives amino_acid_group
#> 1      G1A            1              4        Aliphatic
#> 2      G1D            3              4           Acidic
#> 3      G1S            1              4            Polar
#> 4      G1V            4              4        Aliphatic
#> 5      S2C            2              4            Polar
#> 6      S2F            3              4         Aromatic

Multiple alternatives at residue 156

The reference has L at mature residue 156. In this expanded panel there are five alternative amino acids, each counted separately:

focus_states <- subset(hla_a_evidence(hla)$states, position == 156)
knitr::kable(focus_states[, c("ref", "alt", "is_reference", "allele_count")],
             col.names = c("Reference", "Observed", "Reference match", "Named alleles"))
Reference Observed Reference match Named alleles
856 L F FALSE 2
857 L L TRUE 3172
858 L M FALSE 1
859 L Q FALSE 1184
860 L R FALSE 596
861 L W FALSE 1043 
stopifnot(sum(focus_states$allele_count) == nrow(hla_a_evidence(hla)$alleles))

There are 3,172 reference matches, plus L156F (2), L156M (1), L156Q (1,184), L156R (596), and L156W (1,043). These sum to 5,998. Reference matches remain in the state table and are not substitution heads.

plots$focus

Five amino-acid alternatives sharing one residue anchor. Heights use the same log10(count + 1) convention as the overview; labels show exact original counts.

Each summary row includes up to three example allele names. The complete manifest and source sequences retain all eligible alleles without producing unwieldy lists of thousands of names in each table cell.

Project onto the reference exon–intron model

The same 1,212 substitutions can be placed above the eight coding exons and seven introns of A*02:01:01:01. The bundled IPD HLA00005 reference snapshot comes from the same database release. Its spliced CDS translates exactly to our 365-residue reference precursor followed by a stop codon.

The genomic view uses allele-local HLA00005 coordinates, not GRCh38 chromosome coordinates. It shows the coding region from ATG to stop; untranslated flanks are outside the displayed model. Other alleles’ substitutions are projected onto this one reference structure, not onto separate allele-specific intron models.

knitr::kable(hla_a_gene_structure(hla),
  col.names = c("Feature", "Number", "Start", "End", "Length (bp)"))
Feature Number Start End Length (bp)
1 exon 1 301 373 73
9 intron 1 374 503 130
2 exon 2 504 773 270
10 intron 2 774 1014 241
3 exon 3 1015 1290 276
11 intron 3 1291 1890 600
4 exon 4 1891 2166 276
12 intron 4 2167 2265 99
5 exon 5 2266 2382 117
13 intron 5 2383 2820 438
6 exon 6 2821 2853 33
14 intron 6 2854 2995 142
7 exon 7 2996 3043 48

8 exon 8 3213 3217 5

Store the genomic projection

The exon model and hla_substitutions are already attached to hla. Run the projection verb before building the plot. With store = TRUE, it returns the updated Syn object and attaches a named genomic annotation:

hla <- project_mutations_to_genome(
  hla, annotation = "hla_substitutions", transcripts = "HLA_A0201_tx",
  store = TRUE, name = "hla_genomic"
)
class(get_annotation(hla, "hla_genomic"))
#> [1] "SynGenomicProjectionAnnotation"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ggexon"

This verb converts amino-acid positions to genomic base pairs. It reads precursor positions and follows the selected transcript’s CDS blocks. The original protein annotation, including its mature-coordinate columns, remains available for the preceding protein view.

For a codon crossing a splice junction, the stored projection retains each exonic fragment and one marker anchor on the longest fragment. For example:

Mature residue 1 → precursor residue 25 → genomic fragments 373 and 504–505.

Inspect the stored result directly, without projecting again:

knitr::kable(unique(subset(
  query_genomic_projection(hla, "hla_genomic"), mature_position == 1,
  select = c("mature_position", "position", "seqnames", "xmin", "xmax")
)), col.names = c("Mature residue", "Precursor residue", "Reference sequence",
                  "Genomic start (bp)", "Genomic end (bp)"), row.names = FALSE)
Mature residue Precursor residue Reference sequence Genomic start (bp) Genomic end (bp)
1 25 HLA00005 373 373
1 25 HLA00005 504 505

The marker anchor for this split codon is 504.5, the centre of bases 504–505. It lies on coding sequence even though the codon crosses an intron.

Project the attached protein regions through the same reference CDS. Their stored boundaries also use precursor positions. The projection splits each region into its exonic fragments:

hla <- project_domains_to_genome(
  hla, annotation = "hla_regions", transcripts = "HLA_A0201_tx",
  store = TRUE, name = "hla_genomic_regions"
)

Prepare one layout for every layer

Prepare intron spacing and head positions on the same object. intron_factor sets the shared exon-union map; head_spread bounds the sideways fanning of alternatives sharing an anchor. The verb computes the stems from those same anchors and head positions. Heights retain the existing log10(count + 1) convention; the exon model sits below count 1.

hla <- prepare_genomic_layout(
  hla, annotation = "hla_genomic", name = "hla_lollipops",
  intron_factor = 3, head_spread = 4.8,
  mutation_y_by = "allele_count", mutation_y_trans = "log10",
  mutation_y_range = log10(c(1, 4667) + 1),
  track_ymin = -0.34, track_ymax = -0.08, stem_points = 24
)

The stored layout keeps original genomic coordinates plus one shared display map. Its head, stem, and exon tables can be inspected with query_genomic_layout(hla, "hla_lollipops", component = "mutations") (or "stems" and "exons"). These are views of prepared state, rather than separate inputs that the reader must construct.

Draw the prepared result

All spatial layers and the x scale select genomic_layout = "hla_lollipops". They read the prepared geometry without projecting or spreading positions again. The shared map is applied once across the plot.

Define separate palettes for amino-acid alternatives and protein regions, plus the counts to label on the y axis. Protein regions use six colours from Paul Tol’s Bright qualitative palette, so neighbouring regions differ in hue:

aa_colours <- c(
  Aliphatic = "#E69F00", Aromatic = "#56B4E9", Polar = "#009E73",
  Basic = "#CC79A7", Acidic = "#D55E00", `Gly / Pro` = "#0072B2"
)
region_colours <- c(
  `Alpha-1` = "#4477AA", `Alpha-2` = "#EE6677", `Alpha-3` = "#228833",
  `Connecting peptide` = "#CCBB44", Transmembrane = "#66CCEE", Cytoplasmic = "#AA3377"
)
count_breaks <- c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 5000)

Build the plot directly from hla. geom_exon2() draws the prepared exon model; geom_motif() overlays the projected protein regions at the same height; geom_protein_lollipop() draws the anchored stems and heads. The region blocks use the same intron map as the exon model. Grey bases represent the signal peptide and stop codon, outside the mature-protein regions. The exon-number labels read the stored exon coordinates from the same object. The code below includes all colours, axis labels, and theme settings used in the rendered figure:

genomic_plot <- ggexon(hla) +
  geom_exon2(
    genomic_layout = "hla_lollipops",
    intron_shape = "chevron", intron_peak = 0.12,
    fill = "#DDE3E8", colour = "#8193A1", linewidth = 0.35,
    transcript_backbone_colour = "#647E8A", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_motif(
    aes(fill = motif), annotation = "hla_genomic_regions",
    genomic_layout = "hla_lollipops", colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_protein_lollipop(
    genomic_layout = "hla_lollipops", score = "amino_acid_group",
    show_backbone = FALSE, show_domains = FALSE,
    stem_colour = NULL, stem_linewidth = 0.14, stem_alpha = 0.27,
    point_size = 0.65, point_alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = function(model) query_genomic_layout(model, "hla_lollipops", "exons"),
    aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, label = exon_number),
    y = -0.53, size = 8 / ggplot2::.pt, colour = "#344854",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_ggexon_genomic(
    genomic_layout = "hla_lollipops",
    guide = guide_x_ggexon_piecewise(by = "panel")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    "Alternative amino acid", values = aa_colours,
    breaks = names(aa_colours), drop = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    "Protein region", values = region_colours,
    breaks = names(region_colours), drop = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = log10(count_breaks + 1),
    labels = scales::label_comma()(count_breaks),
    limits = c(-0.8, log10(5001) + 0.18),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.035, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "HLA-A  /  variants on the gene model",
    subtitle = "5,998 named alleles    /    1,212 substitutions    /    8 coding exons + 7 introns    /    introns ÷ 3",
    x = "Reference allele A*02:01:01:01  /  HLA00005 allele-local genomic coordinates",
    y = "Allele count (log scale)",
    caption = paste0(
      "Stem anchors follow the reference CDS, including splice-split codons. ",
      "The numbered coding-exon model spans ATG to stop.\n",
      "Coloured exon segments show mature-protein regions; grey bases are outside them.\n",
      "Exons at native scale; intron gaps ÷ 3. Scale bars show actual base-pair lengths. ",
      "Database counts, not population frequencies."
    )
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1, order = 1, override.aes = list(size = 2.4, alpha = 1)),
    fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1, order = 2)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10, base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#E5E9EC", linewidth = 0.3),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "#5E6C78"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#344854"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 23, face = "bold", colour = "#203747", margin = margin(b = 7)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, colour = "#5E6C78", margin = margin(b = 18)),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9, hjust = 0, colour = "#697884", margin = margin(t = 14)
    ),
    plot.title.position = "plot", plot.caption.position = "plot",
    legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(9, "mm"),
    plot.margin = margin(16, 18, 12, 14)
  )
genomic_plot

Amino-acid substitutions and protein regions are projected through the same reference CDS. Region blocks split at splice junctions and occupy the full exon height. One shared genomic map compresses introns three-fold while preserving exon lengths.

Here geom_protein_lollipop() uses the stored genomic layout. Its ordinary mode still draws protein coordinates; the selected layout makes this choice explicit. Optional geom_mutation_label(genomic_layout = "hla_lollipops") reads the same head positions, so labels cannot acquire a different spread.

Change intron compression or head spacing by running prepare_genomic_layout() again. The scale reads the prepared map, and exon layers disable their own schematic compression. An intron of 600 bp occupies 200 exon-scale units; a 276-bp exon still occupies 276. Use intron_factor = 1 during preparation for an uncompressed view. Changing source mutations or CDS structure requires projection and layout preparation again; stale prepared state raises an error.

Rectangles run from start - 0.5 to end + 0.5, the edges of the first and last base. This makes a 73-base exon exactly 73 coordinate units wide and the first intron exactly 130, avoiding an off-by-one error from inclusive endpoints. Codon anchors retain their original genomic base-centre coordinates. The guide reports 73 bp for the representative exon and 130 bp for the intron.

Reproduce and customize

From the repository root:

python3 data-raw/hla_a_lollipop/build-hla-a-demo.py
Rscript data-raw/hla_a_lollipop/verify-hla-a-demo.R
Rscript data-raw/hla_a_lollipop/verify-hla-a-gene-model.R
Rscript data-raw/hla_a_lollipop/render-hla-a-figure.R

The builder pins the source commit and checks all selected sequences against the official gapped alignment. The renderer exports overview and close-up and gene-model vector PDF and PNG files, substitution counts, projected codon segments, and all residue-state counts to data-raw/hla_a_lollipop/preview.

Edit hla_a_plot_parameters in plot-hla-a-example.R to adjust canvas dimensions, font size, head size, stem opacity, or the maximum local fan width. The default 240 × 135 mm canvas provides space for the dense overview. Every substitution is drawn in both the vector and raster exports.

Sources and attribution

  • IPD-IMGT/HLA release 3.66.0, pinned source repository. Original FASTA records retain their headers, sequences, and line wrapping. IPD-LICENCE.md retains the data terms; the package MIT license does not replace these terms. Counts are computed analyses of original records.
  • Barker DJ et al. The IPD-IMGT/HLA Database: recent developments in sequence submission. Nucleic Acids Research (2026), 54(D1): D1152–D1158.
  • Robinson J, Barker D, Marsh SGE. 25 years of the IPD-IMGT/HLA Database. HLA (2024), 103(6): e15549.
  • Robinson J et al. IMGT/HLA — a sequence database for the human major histocompatibility complex. Tissue Antigens (2000), 55:280–287.
  • UniProt P04439: shared structural regions, under CC BY 4.0. The original snapshot and source SHA-256 values are bundled.
  • IPD alignment conventions: mature-protein numbering and alignment symbols.
